"While both sides appear determined to keep fighting, they have avoided a return to all-out war over the past week."

First of all, the US President explicitly denies the US is at war with Iran — which constitutionally would require an act of Congress, where it would not pass — instead calling the hostilities of the past 5 months a "mere excursion"

2nd, the war has never been "all out". Most notably, the US has avoided using any ground forces or occupying any Iranian territory. Including against Kharg Island, despite repeated threats. It also mostly keeps its navy at a safe distance. The carrier strike groups are operating from up to 600 miles away. And the US mostly avoids attacking Iranian energy infrastructure, and in return Iran mostly doesn't attack the energy infrastructure of the US's Gulf State allies. So it has been far from "all out" since the start.

What we're seeing is the US rely on bombing operations and Iran responding by firing at US bases and the facilities of the country's that host them. That's the case now as it has been since February.

comments.body:
Market behavior as it pertains to health care is very different from market behavior as it pertains to, say, bananas.

The price I am willing to pay for a banana reflects the value I place on eating a banana, as opposed to an apple or an orange.

If, on the other hand, I need health care, I do not have the choice of forgoing it in the same way I can eat an apple instead of an expensive banana. I either get the care, and deal with the financial consequences later, or I forgo the care because I can’t afford it.

If I need a particular thing electively, an MRI, say, and I have a choice, yes, I will take the less expensive choice. But this kind of choice represents a relatively small portion of health care spending. When you’re in an ambulance with a heart attack, or lying unconscious in the ICU in septic shock, price transparency has relatively little effect.

To hedge against these situations, we buy health insurance. It is then the insurers who occupy the marketplace that drives what doctors and hospitals charge, and what they actually get paid.

But in this marketplace, health insurers seek to maximize profit, not quality of health care. And providers seek to maximize reimbursement. The market serves to balance these interests, and leaves health care as a byproduct.

Market forces do not work. We are already spending $5T/year in the health care sector. Best to spend it on health care, without siphoning off profits for shareholders.

That's why we, in the history of capitalist development, have the independent producer on a small plot of land before we have a gigantic  Amazon Warehouse in which the collective labor of many is exploited for profit by a few. 

Allowing prices to go unchecked, simply following the quantitative number that a price sends, completely elides our eroding quality of life, where housing, healthcare, education, food, and water are treated merely as commodities, rather than rights we are all morally entitled to. We can't flourish without these rights. 

You mention laws that prevent monopolization of the healthcare industry, but these laws will merely be spritzing gasoline on the wildfire that is the stunted conversation political economists force us to have when they ignore the only half of the equation that matters-that which we need as social beings in order to develop fully as individuals, who can then contribute meaningfully to our development, over not just long, but healthy lives.

The Grenfell fire is the most telling incident, because despite all the "planning" and "review" it (and many others) still failed to meet basic fire safety standards.  All the government overhead did not make it safer, just more expensive.  On the other hand lack of obvious inspection and maintenance standards allowed the Surfside collapse in Miami (a gap now apparently corrected).

So what is the answer?  Clearly stated objective goals for the approval process, and a process to challenge those goals.  Then rules that every planning requirement must be directly tied to those goals, and a process to challenge both if the requirement does indeed support the goals and if the goal is inadequately supported by maintenance requirements.   Do not allow local politicians or owners to go by what they "feel" is "right" for them.  Do not allow every local to have their own subjective rules.  Make the requirements open, transparent and subject to technical and legal review.  

Consider that the Grenfell tower would not have come close to meeting US national fire safety standards, and no insurance company would have covered it, and no certificate of occupancy would have been (properly) issued  as a result.  But it was apparently just fine, until it obviously wasn't.

China's "open source" approach to AI technology may not be as ironic as your columnist suggests.  China is, after all, the "People's" Republic, and it has been the world's most successful practitioner in striving to improve people's lives. Open source is sharing, and China, in word and action, shows the world's resources are not for an elite few, but are meant to be shared.  Hence, Xi's attempt to limit the wealth and influence of Chinese technocrats. 

 It is amusing, but simplistic, to suggest that an "authoritarian state" is acting for the people by taking the open source approach while America, a supposed democratic nation, is doing the opposite. This kind of black-and-white, good-and-bad type of thinking has become so deeply embedded in the US since the Chinese revolution that even some of your most profound writers offer it as auto-fill in a kind of knee-jerk journalism.

Again, in the person of Xi Jinping, China indicates that it is on the right path. Calm, cool, and collected, Xi is suggesting that AI should be for everybody, an unspoken acknowledgment that, as a collection and synthesis of global data, it actually derives from everyone.

China's open-source approach is not a matter of an authoritarian state ironically defying its evil nature, but, as is often the case, of a successful, independent state defying US stereotypes.

In the days before AC, standard male dress in British tropical colonies consisted of short-sleeved shirts, "tailored" (as they called them) shorts, knee socks -- and sometimes a necktie.  The look hung on in a few places (back in the 80s as a  banker, I paid a call on  a government office in Darwin, Australia and that's how  the men were dressed.)
 Baden-Powell outfitted his newly established Boy Scouts in this style -- soon copied by elite British schools -- and then in Japan  in an era when Japan looked to Britain as a model.  The outfit  became standard wear for Japanese grade school boys.  But shorts  acquired a "boys clothes'' aura so you got the absurdity of grade school boys required to wear shorts in the mid-winter while their older brothers sweated in regulation long trousers in  mid-summer and no Japanese man would ever wear shorts except at the beach or the gym.   That's been changing -- and it's good thing. It's perfectly possible -- as the photos accompanying the article demonstrate  -- to look appropriately serious for an office environment while dressed in neat shorts and short-sleeved shirts.  The Brits managed it a century ago in the Federated Malay States and it wouldn't surprise me to see the fashion-forward Japanese bringing on an updated version of menswear that is both sensible for hot, humid weather and allows the wearer to look professional.

The only chatbot I have to interact with is Strava.  It gives me praise for riding faster .

It encourages 'weekly goals'.  It offers to 'tell me more.'  It does not get upset that I rebuff its advances every time.

Then, the app is ready to track many stats: Power, heartbeat, VO2 max, cadence, calories burned. 
It wants me to rate 'how the ride felt.' It probably would like to check my muscle density and suggest I change diet.

I am starting to wonder why I pay it.  And, who sets its expectations about what is good.  It needs to have a priorities synthesiser like old time sound mixers;  I don't need to improve.  Just stay able to ride.  I don't want a love affair with my phone.  

I do like how it sums up the ride, distilling the pace and distance into a few sentences.  At my age, the records do not get better; they maintain or get slower.  The excitement of seeing my PR's and the standing on the leaderboard has been replaced by 'I could just use my cyclocomputer to track this and no one would know my ride.' But, the people I ride with are all on it,  I see their efforts and they mine.  I like to see their pictures.  When the subscription runs out, I will wait for the discount offer then sign up for another year.  But not for 'tell me more.'  

Here is to hoping that the dopamine hit loses its power for the younger generation, who do not know what driving across the country with only a map, asking directions, and asking people is like, nor will ever know. .

Think about it purely from common sense...

Time on technology - engaging with A.I., ChatGPT, ChatBots, etc. - doesn't provide you tangible experience.

And that is why we are here...to have a human expereince with ourselves and with one another.

That is, actually, how human beings evolve...expereince.

We are physical beings in a physical body, in a physical world...our "physics" matters most.

That's not "woo-woo," it's common sense; of which we now have a dearth of...predominantly due to the over-use of technology.

We have made our "tools" our master. 

Time to take our power - and our humanity - back.

In my early to mid-fifties I began running farther and easier than ever, which came as quite a surprise as I had come through two episodes of cancer and 3 heart attacks during the previous 15 years, with the second episode with cancer involving a stage 4+ tumour surrounding my spinal cord and extending into the bone and muscles of my left hip and thigh--and being told I was going to lose that leg.
Yet training at the gym and on the roads led me to becoming as fit as I had ever been and running farther and easier than ever.
What had changed was my mind set, as I was now running for fun rather than as training for other sports, and I reminded myself that I was doing something I was told I would never do again as I began each run.
Mind and body, one and the same.
